column2: An electron microscope forms its image from a beam of electrons interacting with the specimen.
A fluorescent label takes in light and emits light of a different wavelength, making its target stand out.
A confocal microscope can build a sharp optical section by scanning the sample one spot at a time.
As an electron beam scans the surface, signals from each spot build up a picture of the specimen.
A spot of mixed pigments can spread into separate bands as solvent travels along the paper.
A carrier gas moves a vaporized sample through a column, and its components emerge at different times.
A thin coating of silica on a plate can separate a mixture into a trail of distinct spots.
A flowing liquid carries the sample past a stationary material that retains some components longer than others.
Polyacrylamide forms a porous gel through which charged molecules migrate under an electric field.
Agar or agarose forms the gel that holds the sample while an electric field separates its components.
A protein stops moving along the pH gradient when it reaches the pH at which its net charge is zero.
A thin capillary acts as a separation lane for charged molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids.
In a color-based ELISA, an enzyme tag turns antibody binding into a color change that a reader can measure.
After proteins move from a gel onto a membrane, an antibody can pick out a specific protein band.
A radioactively labeled tracer makes it possible to measure how much material binds to an antibody.
Two short primers mark the ends of the DNA segment that a polymerase copies in successive cycles.
Whole genome sequencing reads DNA across an organism’s genome, including regions between genes.
A karyotype arranges a cell’s chromosomes so that their number and overall structure can be examined.
A DNA profile combines patterns at several variable sites to distinguish one sample from another.
A hematocrit of 40% means red cells occupy about four tenths of the blood sample’s volume.
A blood cell count reports how many cells occur in a measured volume of blood.
A white cell count gives a total, and a differential breaks that total down by cell type.
A platelet count reports how many of these clot-forming cell fragments occupy a measured volume of blood.
A red cell count measures the number of red cells in a volume of blood, even when the cells vary in size.
An X-ray detector records a shadow image because tissues absorb different amounts of the beam.
MRI reconstructs an image from radio signals emitted by atomic nuclei in a strong magnetic field.
An ultrasound image maps echoes that return when a sound pulse encounters a boundary between tissues.
CT combines X-ray measurements from many angles to reconstruct a slice through the body.
A PET tracer can show where cells are taking up a labeled molecule such as a glucose analogue.
Mammography uses X-rays to show structures within breast tissue.
Returning ultrasound echoes can show the heart’s valves moving as its chambers fill and empty.
A culture lets researchers maintain or grow living cells outside their original tissue.
A cell count can describe cells per unit of fluid or cells within a measured area of tissue.
A flow cytometer measures individual cells as they cross a light beam, recording signals such as fluorescence and scattered light.
Fixation preserves the arrangement of tissue so that its cells can still be studied after processing.
Silver salts create contrast that can bring fine structures into view in a tissue section.
In negative staining, material around a particle takes up the stain and outlines the particle against a dark background.
Patterns of stained bands give individual chromosomes recognizable landmarks for spotting rearrangements.
An ultracentrifuge can subject a sample to a field more than 100,000 times Earth’s gravity.
Insulin signals the liver to slow glucose production, helping lower the amount of glucose circulating in blood.
Luteinizing hormone signals Leydig cells in the testes to produce testosterone.
The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine, which can make the heart beat faster and widen the airways.
Estradiol is a steroid hormone with an 18-carbon skeleton and a hydroxyl group at each of two sites.
The corpus luteum produces progesterone after ovulation to help prepare the uterus for implantation.
Alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon, which signals the liver to release glucose into the blood.
Somatotropin is another name for the growth hormone released by the anterior pituitary.
Hydrocortisone is the chemical name for cortisol, a glucocorticoid produced by the adrenal cortex.
Estrogens act through receptors in tissues such as the uterus, where they support growth of its lining.
Oxytocin released by the posterior pituitary triggers the contractions that eject milk from the breast.
The anterior pituitary releases prolactin, which supports milk production in mammary tissue.
Arginine vasopressin helps the kidneys conserve water and has just nine amino acids.
Gastrin released in the stomach stimulates secretion of gastric acid.
The lining of the duodenum releases secretin, which signals the pancreas to release bicarbonate-rich fluid.
Cholecystokinin helps digestion by contracting the gallbladder and stimulating pancreatic enzyme release.
Bright light falling on the retina can trigger the iris muscles to narrow the pupil.
In the knee jerk, a quick stretch of the quadriceps triggers that same muscle to contract.
Stimulating sensory receptors near the soft palate can trigger a contraction of the throat muscles.
A reflex blink briefly closes the eyelids to shield the surface of the eye.
Respiratory rate counts breathing cycles, usually over one minute.
Tidal volume measures how much air moves with one quiet breath.
After the deepest possible inhalation, the air a person can breathe out is their vital capacity.
Total lung capacity includes the air that stays in the lungs even after a full exhalation.
Heart rate counts ventricular beats over time and is usually reported in beats per minute.
Arterial pressure changes through the heartbeat, giving a higher systolic and a lower diastolic reading.
Multiplying the volume pumped per beat by the number of beats per minute gives cardiac output.
Total circulating blood volume includes both the plasma and the cells carried in it.
Digestion breaks food down into smaller components that the body can absorb and use.
Chewing mechanically breaks food into smaller pieces before swallowing.
Deglutition is the coordinated movement that carries a mouthful of food or liquid into the esophagus.
A wave of muscle contraction can move a bolus of food along the esophagus.
Salivary glands release fluid that moistens the mouth and helps begin digestion.
The rods and cones of the retina convert incoming light into signals the nervous system can use.
Separate temperature-sensitive nerve endings in the skin can signal cooling and warming.
Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging stimuli, including intense heat or mechanical force.
The hair cells that respond to vibration in the inner ear are a form of mechanoreceptor.
Chemoreceptors can detect changes inside the body as well as chemicals entering the nose or mouth.
Whole blood contains cells suspended in a liquid component called plasma.
The kidneys produce urine, which travels through the ureters to the bladder.
Saliva contains both slippery mucins and an enzyme that begins breaking down starch.
Sweat carries dissolved salts, including sodium chloride, onto the skin.
Spinning blood that has been kept from clotting separates its cells from its liquid plasma.
Tissue fluid takes the name lymph once it enters the lymphatic vessels.
The choroid plexus produces fluid that circulates through the brain’s ventricles and around the brain and spinal cord.
Activated factor VIII helps factor IXa activate factor X on a membrane surface during clot formation.
Thrombin cuts soluble fibrinogen to produce the fibrin strands that give a clot its meshwork.
Prothrombin circulates as an inactive precursor until the clotting cascade converts it into thrombin.
Activated factor IX works together with factor VIIIa to activate factor X in the clotting cascade.
IgG accounts for the largest share of antibodies in normal human serum.
Secretory IgA reaches mucosal surfaces in fluids such as saliva.
IgM can activate the complement cascade after it binds its target.
Helper T cells coordinate immune responses, while cytotoxic T cells can kill infected cells.
An activated B cell can give rise to plasma cells that secrete antibodies.
Several routes into the complement system converge on cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b.
When C5 splits, C5a signals inflammation and C5b helps start assembly of a membrane-piercing complex.
C1 contains three different components, called C1q, C1r and C1s.
Activated C1s cleaves C4 early in the classical complement pathway.
A fragment of C2 joins C4b to build the enzyme that cleaves C3 in the classical pathway.
Interleukins carry signals that can prompt white blood cells to divide or develop new functions.
Interferon signals can turn on antiviral defenses in nearby cells.
Activated macrophages release TNF-alpha, an inflammatory signal whose name reflects its effects on tumor cells.
IL-6 can support the growth and differentiation of B cells.
Activated T cells release IL-2, which stimulates lymphocytes to multiply.
Activated lymphocytes can release interferon-gamma, which helps macrophages respond to microbes.
Small, often bean-shaped lymph nodes sit along the paths of lymphatic vessels.
The spleen filters circulating blood through tissue enclosed in a capsule.
The thymus sits behind the breastbone and provides a place for T cells to mature.
The two palatine tonsils sit on opposite sides of the throat between folds of the soft palate.
A phagocyte surrounds a particle with its membrane, enclosing the particle for breakdown inside the cell.
An antigen can stimulate B cells to multiply and differentiate into antibody-producing cells.
An antigen-presenting cell can display a peptide on its surface for a T cell to recognize.
A resting lymphocyte can enlarge and begin dividing after it receives an activating signal.
In autoimmune type 1 diabetes, loss of insulin-producing beta cells leaves the pancreas unable to supply enough insulin.
Rheumatoid arthritis inflames the synovium, the tissue lining a movable joint.
Systemic lupus can involve several tissues in the same illness, including skin, joints and kidneys.
In Graves disease, antibodies can stimulate the thyroid’s TSH receptor and increase hormone production.
Immune attack on thyroid tissue in Hashimoto disease can reduce the gland’s hormone output.
Anaphylaxis can affect the skin, breathing and circulation during the same rapid allergic reaction.
In allergic rhinitis, an allergen triggers inflammation in the lining of the nose.
An immune reaction to a food can affect the skin as well as the digestive tract.
Peanut allergy occurs when the immune system reacts to proteins from the peanut.
After sensitization, renewed skin contact with the same substance can produce an inflammatory rash.
The strains selected for seasonal flu vaccines are reviewed as circulating influenza viruses change.
Different COVID-19 vaccines can present a viral protein directly or carry instructions for making it.
MMR combines protection against three distinct viruses in one vaccine.
Polio vaccines include an injected inactivated form and an oral live attenuated form.
Tetanus toxoid is an inactivated form of the bacterial toxin that can still elicit antibodies against it.
Recombinant hepatitis B vaccines present a viral surface protein to the immune system.
HPV vaccines target types of papillomavirus linked to cervical cancer and other cancers.
Members of Escherichia are rod-shaped bacteria that can grow with or without oxygen.
Staphylococci divide in several planes and can form irregular clusters of round cells.
Under a microscope, streptococci can appear as pairs or chains of round bacterial cells.
Lactobacilli are rod-shaped bacteria that can produce lactic acid during fermentation.
Different members of the Salmonella genus can cause intestinal infection or enteric fever.
Bacillus bacteria form endospores inside their rod-shaped cells.
Clostridium includes Gram-positive bacteria found in soil and in the intestinal tracts of animals.
Pseudomonas includes aerobic Gram-negative rods that live in the environment as well as in hosts.
Vibrio cells have a curved, rod-like shape that can resemble a comma.
Neisseria are round Gram-negative bacteria, and some species live in the upper airway.
Many E. coli strains live in the intestine without causing disease, while other strains can cause diarrhea.
Staphylococcus aureus can live in the nose or on the skin and can also cause infection.
The pneumococcus can inhabit the upper respiratory tract and can also cause lung infection.
In culture, tuberculosis bacteria can grow side by side in cord-like bundles.
This curved stomach bacterium makes urease, an enzyme that breaks down urea.
Penicillium grows branching, brush-shaped structures that carry its spores.
Some Candida species grow as budding yeasts and can also form elongated chains called pseudohyphae.
Aspergillus molds produce airborne spores that can reach the lungs when inhaled.
Baker’s yeast and brewer’s yeast both belong to the genus Saccharomyces.
The name HIV covers two human immunodeficiency viruses, HIV-1 and HIV-2.
Coronaviruses can infect the respiratory or digestive tract of different vertebrate hosts.
Measles virus belongs to the morbillivirus group of RNA viruses.
The three poliovirus serotypes all belong to the enterovirus group.
Rabies virus can enter through infected saliva and multiply in nerve cells.
SARS-CoV-2 is the coronavirus identified in 2019 as the cause of COVID-19.
The H and N in names such as H1N1 refer to two different surface proteins of influenza A.
Different HPV types can cause warts or contribute to cancers such as cervical cancer.
HSV-1 can persist in sensory ganglia between episodes of active infection.
The intact infectious hepatitis B virus particle is also called a Dane particle.
Human adenoviruses can infect the eye, airway or digestive tract.
Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox on first infection and shingles when it reactivates.
Adult Ascaris roundworms inhabit the intestine of their host.
Taenia is a genus of tapeworms that includes the beef tapeworm and the pork tapeworm.
The human pinworm belongs to the genus Enterobius and lives in the intestine.
A human Ascaris infection can begin when a person swallows eggs containing developing larvae.
Freshwater snails serve as intermediate hosts for Schistosoma blood flukes.
Strongyloides includes roundworms that parasitize the intestines of mammals.
Lambda’s DNA has short complementary ends that let it form a circle inside its bacterial host.
T4 infects E. coli and carries its genetic instructions in double-stranded DNA.
T7 carries linear double-stranded DNA and can break open an E. coli cell to release new phages.
M13 is a long, filament-shaped phage with a single-stranded DNA genome.
Candida yeasts can cause superficial infections of moist tissues, including oral thrush.
Athlete’s foot is a fungal infection of foot skin caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton.
Tinea fungi can infect keratin-containing tissues, including hair and nails.
Aspergillosis is the name for infection caused by molds in the genus Aspergillus.
In a demyelinating form of Guillain-Barré syndrome, the immune response injures the insulation around peripheral nerves.
Alzheimer disease can affect memory, judgment and problem solving as brain function changes over time.
Slowed movement, muscle rigidity and a tremor at rest are characteristic movement changes in Parkinson disease.
Epileptic seizures arise from sudden bursts of abnormal electrical activity in networks of brain cells.
Meningitis affects the membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.
Encephalitis is inflammation within brain tissue and can have an infectious or autoimmune cause.
Huntington disease follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and can produce involuntary movements called chorea.
When iron stores are depleted, red cells can become smaller and carry less hemoglobin.
In sickle cell anemia, hemoglobin S can distort red cells and shorten their lifespan.
In aplastic anemia, bone marrow produces too few blood cells, often affecting several cell types.
Hemolytic anemia develops when red cells break down faster than the body can replace them.
Insomnia can involve difficulty staying asleep even when falling asleep is easy.
Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep can briefly rouse the sleeper and fragment the night’s rest.
Along with daytime sleepiness, some people with narcolepsy experience sudden loss of muscle tone called cataplexy.
Sleepwalking arises during a partial awakening from deep non-REM sleep.
In atrial fibrillation, disorganized electrical activity prevents the atria from contracting together.
In ventricular tachycardia, a rapid rhythm originates in the heart’s lower chambers.
During ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles quiver without producing an effective heartbeat.
In typical atrial flutter, an electrical signal travels repeatedly around a circuit in the right atrium.
A slow heart rate can result from a slow pacemaker in the sinus node or delayed conduction to the ventricles.
In classic phenylketonuria, reduced activity of phenylalanine hydroxylase allows phenylalanine to accumulate.
Galactosemias are inherited disorders in which an enzyme needed to process the sugar galactose is deficient.
In Tay-Sachs disease, deficient hexosaminidase A allows a fatty molecule called GM2 ganglioside to build up in nerve cells.
In Gaucher disease, a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase lets a fatty substance accumulate inside lysosomes.
Too little thyroid hormone can slow the rate at which the body uses energy at rest.
Excess thyroid hormone can raise the body’s resting metabolic rate.
A goiter describes an enlarged thyroid gland, which can produce high, low or normal amounts of hormone.
Keratitis affects the cornea, the transparent tissue at the front of the eye.
A corneal ulcer involves a break in the corneal surface with damage to the underlying tissue.
In keratoconus, the cornea thins and bulges forward into a cone-like shape.
Essential tremor can involve the hands and may also cause the head to shake.
Tourette syndrome involves both motor and vocal tics, which may appear at different times.
Migraine can occur with an aura, a temporary neurological symptom such as a change in vision.
Tension-type headache can feel like a band of pressure around the head.
A cluster headache attack can cause intense pain around one eye, with tearing on that same side.
Cells can break down the six-carbon sugar glucose to obtain energy.
Fructose occurs as a free sugar in honey and fruit.
Galactose is one of the two sugars released when lactose is split.
Ribose is the five-carbon sugar in the backbone of RNA.
One glucose and one fructose join to make a molecule of table sugar.
Lactose in milk contains one glucose unit joined to one galactose unit.
Maltose is a pair of glucose units that can be released as starch breaks down.
Oleic acid has one double bond in an 18-carbon chain.
Palmitic acid has a saturated 16-carbon chain and occurs in palm oil and animal fats.
Stearic acid has an 18-carbon chain with no carbon-carbon double bonds.
Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid whose carbon chain has two double bonds.
NAD can pick up electrons to become NADH and pass them on in another reaction.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups, including the two-carbon acetyl group in acetyl-CoA.
NADP can accept electrons to form NADPH, an electron donor for many biosynthetic reactions.
FAD contains a component derived from riboflavin, also called vitamin B2.
A choline-containing head group distinguishes phosphatidylcholines among membrane phospholipids.
Sphingomyelins have a phosphate-containing head group and occur in the myelin that surrounds nerve fibers.
Phosphatidylserines take their name from the amino acid serine in their head group.
A ribosome reads the sequence of messenger RNA as a template for assembling a protein.
A transfer RNA pairs its anticodon with a messenger RNA codon and brings the corresponding amino acid.
Ribosomal RNA and proteins together make the ribosome, the structure that translates messenger RNA.
A microRNA helps guide a silencing complex to a matching messenger RNA, reducing production of its protein.
ATP has three phosphate groups and can transfer its terminal phosphate to another molecule.
Adding one phosphate to ADP regenerates ATP.
AMP contains adenine, a ribose sugar and one phosphate group.
GTP carries three phosphates on guanosine and serves as an energy source during protein synthesis.
Lipase can free a fatty acid from a triglyceride by breaking an ester bond.
Amylases break bonds between glucose units in starch, producing shorter carbohydrates.
Pepsin A is a protein-cutting enzyme formed from an inactive precursor called pepsinogen.
Trypsin cuts proteins on the carboxyl side of certain lysine and arginine residues.
Lactase splits milk sugar into glucose and galactose.
Acetylcholinesterase breaks the neurotransmitter acetylcholine into choline and acetate.
In transmission electron microscopy, the detector receives electrons that have passed through a thin specimen.
Phase-contrast microscopy turns subtle changes in light passing through a specimen into visible differences in brightness.
Cryo-electron microscopy can image molecules held in a rapidly frozen layer of water.
High pressure drives the liquid mobile phase through the tightly packed column of an HPLC instrument.
An affinity column can capture a protein by binding a particular part of it to a matching ligand.
An ion-exchange column separates molecules by the way their charges interact with the resin.
Changing the direction of the electric field helps a gel separate very large DNA fragments.
A second separation across the first lane spreads a sample into a two-dimensional pattern of spots.
Electrophoresis separates a mixture of blood proteins into bands that include albumin and globulins.
Antibodies can pick out their targets after material from a sample has been transferred onto a membrane.
In an ELISpot assay, a spot can mark where one cell secreted the molecule being measured.
Exome sequencing focuses on exons, the parts of genes retained in mature RNA.
As DNA or RNA passes through a tiny pore, changes in electrical current help reveal its sequence.
Real-time PCR tracks the buildup of amplified DNA while the reaction is still running.
Several primer pairs let a single PCR reaction amplify several different targets.
Prothrombin time measures how long plasma takes to clot after tissue factor and calcium are added.
This test times clot formation in plasma after phospholipid and calcium are added under defined conditions.
Reticulocytes are young red cells, so their count gives a glimpse of recent red cell production.
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate tracks how far red cells settle in a tube over a set time.
Fluoroscopy uses a sequence of X-ray images to show movement within the body.
Contrast material inside blood vessels outlines their paths on an X-ray angiogram.
Echoes from moving red cells return with a frequency shift that can reveal the direction of blood flow.
A SPECT camera detects photons from a tracer at several angles to build a three-dimensional image.
A microtome cuts tissue into thin slices that light can pass through on a microscope slide.
A block of material such as paraffin supports soft tissue while a blade cuts thin sections.
Cryopreservation can keep cells or tissues in storage by cooling them to very low temperatures.
An antibody label can show where a particular protein sits within a tissue section.
The PAS reaction can make carbohydrate-rich structures such as glycogen stores stand out in a tissue section.
A probe binds a matching nucleic acid sequence while the target remains in its original cell or tissue.
A fluorescent probe makes its matching sequence appear as a bright spot on a chromosome.
In an equilibrium density gradient, particles form a band where the surrounding fluid matches their own density.
The four iodine atoms in thyroxine give it the short name T4.
Calcitonin released from thyroid C cells can reduce calcium release from bone.
Aldosterone signals the kidney to retain sodium and increase potassium excretion.
A surge of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary helps trigger ovulation.
FSH from the anterior pituitary supports ovarian follicle growth and sperm production.
The stomach releases ghrelin, a peptide that can stimulate appetite.
Intestinal L cells release GLP-1, which helps amplify insulin secretion when glucose is elevated.
The anterior pituitary releases thyrotropin, also called TSH, to stimulate the thyroid gland.
The Babinski response includes upward movement of the big toe when the sole is stroked.
A sudden loud sound can produce an involuntary blink and a quick contraction of several muscles.
Stretch receptors in arteries signal changes in pressure and help adjust heart rate from beat to beat.
Even after the strongest exhalation, a residual volume of air stays in the lungs.
FEV1 measures the volume of air expelled in the first second of a forced exhalation.
Peak expiratory flow is the highest airflow reached during a forceful breath out.
Stroke volume measures the blood ejected by one ventricle in a single beat.
The pressure inside an artery rises and falls as the heart ejects blood and then relaxes.
Central venous pressure reflects pressure in the large veins near the right side of the heart.
Flow velocity describes how fast blood travels past a point in a vessel.
Gastric emptying moves stomach contents through the pylorus into the first part of the small intestine.
Nutrients can cross the intestinal lining into blood or lymph.
Rods help the retina detect light at levels too low for useful color vision.
Cones with different sensitivities to wavelength allow the retina to distinguish colors.
Muscle spindles lie within skeletal muscle and signal changes in its length.
A taste bud contains groups of sensory cells that respond to dissolved chemicals.
The liver produces bile, whose bile salts help disperse fats during digestion.
Tears form a fluid layer over the cornea and carry antimicrobial proteins such as lysozyme.
Synovial fluid lubricates the surfaces where bones meet in a movable joint.
Semen combines sperm with fluid from accessory glands, including the prostate and seminal vesicles.
Human milk carries secretory antibodies as well as nutrients.
Activated factor V helps factor Xa convert prothrombin into thrombin.
Activated factor VII works with tissue factor near the start of one route into the clotting cascade.
Factor Xa forms part of the enzyme complex that converts prothrombin into thrombin.
IgE can attach to mast cells and participate in rapid allergic responses.
Cytotoxic T cells recognize targets such as infected cells and can trigger their death.
Regulatory T cells can dampen the activity of other immune cells.
Plasma cells develop from B cells and specialize in secreting antibodies.
C1q is the recognition component that can bind antibody complexes at the start of the classical complement pathway.
C3b can attach to a microbial surface and mark it for uptake by a phagocyte.
C5a can draw immune cells toward a site where complement has been activated.
Terminal complement proteins assemble into a pore that disrupts a target cell’s membrane.
In adults the kidneys produce most erythropoietin, which stimulates red cell production in the marrow.
The thoracic duct returns lymph to the circulation near the junction of veins at the base of the neck.
The adenoids are lymphoid tissue high in the throat, behind the nose.
Memory lymphocytes can mount a quicker response when they encounter a previously recognized antigen.
Coating a microbe with an opsonin such as C3b helps phagocytes recognize and engulf it.
Myasthenia gravis impairs signaling where motor nerves meet skeletal muscle and can cause weakness that worsens with use.
Sjögren syndrome can damage the glands that produce tears and saliva.
Inactivated rabies vaccines present viral antigens without a replicating rabies virus.
BCG uses a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis to stimulate immunity against tuberculosis.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa can make pigments, including the blue-green pigment pyocyanin.
Toxin-producing strains of Vibrio cholerae can cause the profuse watery diarrhea of cholera.
Streptococcus pyogenes is also known as group A streptococcus.
Listeria monocytogenes is a rod-shaped bacterium that can live in soil and cause foodborne infection.
Bacillus anthracis forms spores and can cause anthrax in humans and other mammals.
Clostridium tetani produces tetanospasmin, the toxin responsible for the muscle spasms of tetanus.
Norovirus can cause outbreaks of gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea.
Rotavirus particles have a wheel-like appearance when viewed with an electron microscope.
Four distinct serotypes of dengue virus can be transmitted by mosquitoes.
Yellow fever virus reaches people through the bites of infected mosquitoes.
Humans are the natural host for rubella virus.
Mumps virus can cause swelling of the parotid salivary glands near the jaw.
Human herpesvirus 4, also called Epstein–Barr virus, can infect B cells.
Variola virus is the orthopoxvirus that caused smallpox.
Onychomycosis is a nail infection that can be caused by dermatophytes, yeasts or other molds.
Tinea capitis involves the scalp and can invade hair shafts.
ALS damages both upper motor neurons in the brain and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord.
An accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid in hydrocephalus can enlarge the brain’s ventricles.
Cerebral palsy encompasses movement disorders that arise from an injury or disturbance in the developing brain.
Pernicious anemia can develop when a lack of intrinsic factor prevents normal absorption of vitamin B12.
In thalassemia, the body makes too little of one or more of the protein chains in hemoglobin.
In obstructive sleep apnea, air movement stops or falls even as the breathing muscles continue to work.
The urge to move in restless legs syndrome often eases briefly with movement.
An AV block delays or interrupts electrical signals traveling from the atria to the ventricles.
This disorder impairs the breakdown of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine.
In alkaptonuria, accumulated homogentisic acid can cause urine to darken on standing.
Thyroiditis means inflammation of the thyroid gland and includes several conditions with different causes.
Excess fluid can cloud the normally transparent cornea and interfere with vision.
Chorea produces brief, irregular involuntary movements that can seem to flow from one part of the body to another.
A migraine aura can include reversible visual or sensory changes before or during the headache.
The sugar in DNA lacks the hydroxyl group at the 2-prime position found in the ribose of RNA.
Trehalose links two glucose molecules through their anomeric carbons.
Ubiquinone, also called coenzyme Q, carries electrons within the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Cyclic AMP carries signals inside a cell and has one phosphate linked to two positions on its sugar.
Muramidase is another name for lysozyme, an enzyme in tears and saliva that attacks bacterial cell walls.
The pancreas releases inactive chymotrypsinogen, which is activated in the small intestine to help digest proteins.
